text: There would be a light on in my own window and somebody behind it still up.

text: The flat would be cold, and the second cup would be where it has been since March.
I thought about telephoning and could not settle on which number. That is the whole of that.
Nobody was sitting up for me, which makes a night like this one cheaper.
The landlady would have the notice under my door by Monday, typed.
Two weeks in a parked car outside a hotel in Astoria, and the money went on the car.
The rib Tuesday left me had opinions about stairs.
Forty dollars in the coat, and a coat that needed the forty dollars.
Nobody was waiting up for me, which was its own kind of mercy some nights.
I kept a list of people I owed money, and my own name wasn't the shortest line on it.
I ate a good dinner alone and didn't mind it, which surprised me a little.
Money in the pocket and nobody to spend it on but myself. I'd gotten used to that arithmetic.
There was nobody home to notice what state I came in, and some mornings that was the whole problem.
I drank alone most nights now, which either meant I preferred it or had stopped noticing the difference.
Nobody waited up to ask about the bruise, so I didn't have to explain it to anybody but the mirror.
I patched myself up at the kitchen table, same as always, same as nobody watching.
Watching two people take each other apart over a signature had a way of making my own arrangement look sensible.
I went home to an empty room after that case and found the quiet didn't bother me the way it once might have.
An empty apartment doesn't keep you up, but it doesn't help you sleep either.
I counted the cracks in the ceiling instead of sheep, mostly out of habit.
I thought, for half a second, about who I'd tell the good news to, and came up empty.
A fee like that used to mean something to somebody. Now it just meant the rent.
She'd have the coffee on when I got in, and ask about the rent before she asked about the case.
I hadn't told her yet how far behind we were, and I wasn't looking forward to it.
I thought about the look on her face when I laid the fee on the table.
For once I'd be able to walk in with good news instead of an excuse.
She'd smell the whiskey before I got my coat off, and say nothing about it, which was worse.
I practiced what I'd say about the state of me, and none of it sounded any better out loud.
She'd ask about the jaw first and the case second, same as always.
I thought up three different stories for the bruise on the walk over, and used none of them.
After two weeks on that divorce case, going home to someone who wasn't lying to me felt like a favor.
She never asked what the last case had been about, and I never told her. Some arrangements work better that way.
She'd be asleep by now, and I thought about that more than I thought about the case.
I pictured the apartment dark and quiet, and it got me through the last hour easier than coffee would have.
I'd bring her something with this fee, nothing fancy, just something.
She never asked how much a case paid, only whether I was coming home in one piece.
She used to keep better track of the bills than I did. I still hadn't found her system.
The rent had been easier split two ways, back when it was.
I thought about sending her something, then thought better of it, same as usual.
Money never used to sit easy with me either, until there was somebody to spend it on.
She used to say I drank worse when a case went bad. She wasn't wrong, and she isn't here to say it anymore.
I woke up reaching for a glass of water she used to leave on the nightstand, out of habit more than memory.
She used to patch me up better than I patch myself up now.
Nobody left to ask about the bruise, which I told myself was easier.
I took the divorce work maybe because it was easier than admitting my own hadn't gone any better.
Watching that couple fight over furniture reminded me I never did get my books back from her.
Some nights I still reached for her side of the bed before I remembered.
The apartment was quieter since she left, and I still hadn't decided if that was a mercy.
I used to split good news two ways. Now I just banked it.
She'd have known exactly what to do with a fee like this. I still hadn't worked it out.
She'd lend me the rent if I asked. I wasn't going to ask. We both knew it anyway.
I owed her more than the landlady, one way or another, and neither debt was getting paid soon.
I thought about calling her with the good news, then remembered why I usually didn't.
Money made things easier between us for about a day, historically. I wasn't holding my breath this time.
She always said the drinking was a symptom, not the problem. I never asked what she thought the problem was.
I'd have called her, hungover as I was, if I thought it would go anywhere good.
She'd have plenty to say about the bruise, none of it comforting, all of it probably true.
I decided not to mention the jaw to her, which she'd have called typical, and been right to.
The divorce case had a way of making me count up everything unresolved in my own life, which was a long list.
She'd have found it funny, me working a case like that, given our own history.
I lay awake running arguments we'd already had, improving my side of them after the fact.
She used to say I only missed her at the worst hour of the night. She wasn't wrong about the timing.
I thought about what she'd say about the fee, and decided I already knew, and didn't call.
Good news and complicated people don't mix well over the telephone. I'd learned that one the hard way.
The hangover stung less when there was nobody around to disapprove of it.
I practiced the number in my head so it wouldn't come out wrong when she asked.
Four in the morning was when I missed her most, and I'd stopped pretending otherwise.
I wondered if anyone could sum up the pair of us as neatly as I'd just summed up that couple's wreck of a marriage.
